newsitem.title: FRANCE: French market watchdog wants firms to come clean.
newsitem.headline: French market watchdog wants firms to come clean.

text.p: The French stock market's watchdog COB on Tuesday took a further step in its campaign to stamp out insider dealing and encourage more corporate information by demanding greater honesty among directors.

Companies could no longer stay silent for strategic reasons while the markets were reacting to detailed rumours, chairman Michel Prada of the Commission des Operations de Bourse wrote in the COB's annual report.

He made no direct reference to AXA's takeover of UAP, a merger between Lyonnaise des Eaux and Cie de Suez or Generale des Eaux increasing its stake in Havas, all of which were circulating in some detail in the share market before the deals were confirmed.

Prada wrote that directors, when asked to comment on a rumour, could decline to comment "unless the rumours become detailed and are in line with the project for which official statements are planned later in time."
"It becomes necessary to make a statement because it is manifest that the confidentiality of information is no longer assured," the report said.
Private retailer Auchan, when it had taken a 10 percent stake in Docks de France, denied planning a bid on the shares. The same year it did make a share bid.
Holding company Cerus during 1996 often denied it had put its stake in Valeo on sale, until it sold it to CGIP.
In May 1996, Generale des Eaux denied it wanted to increase its stake in Havas but in February 1997 it became the biggest shareholder in Havas after a share swap concerning Canal Plus.

AXA chairman Claude Bebear in September 1996 denied in front of financial analysts that his company wanted to take over UAP. In November the two companies announced a mega-merger to create the second-largest insurer in the world.
Talk about a pending Lyonnaise des Eaux merger with Suez had been swirling in the market for many weeks before either of the companies made an official statement confirming discussions were underway.
COB said that due to the "increase in the speed of the restructuring of the economy" it was necessary to sharpen its rules concerning public information.

It maintained its key rule that the public needs to be informed as soon as possible. A company may stay quiet a while when publication would hurt its "legitimite interests" but must act when confidentiality is no longer assured.

The COB is also trying to make financial information about French companies more in line with other international markets so that comparisons become more easier, and it repeated its stance that it favoured a harmonisation of international accounting rules.
The COB is setting up a financial information database, named Sophie, which will be accessible via the Internet.
